title: 1 Kings 13:20–34
context: At the table, the LORD's word comes to the very prophet who lied, announcing that because the man of God disobeyed, his body will not be buried with his fathers. On the way home a lion kills him but does not eat him or the donkey, a sign that this is God's judgment rather than chance. The old prophet buries him in his own tomb, mourns him, and asks to be buried beside him, affirming that the word against Bethel will come true. Yet Jeroboam does not turn from his evil way, and this becomes the sin that destroys his house. The phrase "cities of Samaria" in verse 32 may reflect the writer's later vantage, since the city of Samaria is built later (16:24); that observation is offered as a possibility, not a certainty.

verses.text: As they sat at the table, the LORD’s word came to the prophet who brought him back;
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD's word comes to the prophet who brought him back. Arminian readers note the irony that God speaks a true word through the very man who lied, showing that God's word is not bound by the speaker's character.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God remains sovereign over his word, even using a deceiver as its messenger. The true word now exposes the false one and pronounces judgment.

verses.text: and he cried out to the man of God who came from Judah, saying, “The LORD says, ‘Because you have been disobedient to the LORD’s word, and have not kept the commandment which the LORD your God commanded you,
verses.arminianNotes: "Because you have been disobedient to the LORD's word." Arminian readers see the man of God held responsible for his choice, even though he was deceived; he had God's clear command and set it aside.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God holds his servant accountable for disobeying a direct command. Being deceived does not remove responsibility when God's word was plain.

verses.text: but came back, and have eaten bread and drank water in the place of which he said to you, “Eat no bread, and drink no water,” your body will not come to the tomb of your fathers.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: "Your body will not come to the tomb of your fathers." Arminian readers note the severity of the sentence, which concerns his death and burial far from home, not necessarily his eternal destiny.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the judgment is temporal: death and burial away from his family's tomb. The text does not speak to his eternal state, and both traditions avoid speculation on that question.

verses.text: After he had eaten bread and after he drank, he saddled the donkey for the prophet whom he had brought back.
verses.arminianNotes: After the meal, the old prophet saddles the donkey for him. Arminian readers note the unsettling hospitality that follows the pronouncement of judgment, as the man of God sets out toward its fulfillment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the quiet narration as the man of God departs. God's word has been spoken, and the following verses will show it coming to pass on the road.

verses.text: When he had gone, a lion met him by the way and killed him. His body was thrown on the path, and the donkey stood by it. The lion also stood by the body.
verses.arminianNotes: A lion kills him; the body lies on the path with the donkey and lion standing by. Arminian readers see the seriousness of disobedience among those entrusted with God's word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the extraordinary scene: the lion kills but does not eat or attack the donkey. God governs even wild animals to mark this death as his judgment, not an accident.

verses.text: Behold, men passed by and saw the body thrown on the path, and the lion standing by the body; and they came and told it in the city where the old prophet lived.
verses.arminianNotes: Passersby see the body and the lion standing by and report it in the city. Arminian readers note that the scene becomes a public sign, so that people in Bethel can see God's word confirmed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God makes the judgment visible and public. The unusual scene testifies to Bethel that the word against its altar comes from the LORD.

verses.text: When the prophet who brought him back from the way heard of it, he said, “It is the man of God who was disobedient to the LORD’s word. Therefore the LORD has delivered him to the lion, which has mauled him and slain him, according to the LORD’s word which he spoke to him.”
verses.arminianNotes: The old prophet interprets the death as God's judgment "according to the LORD's word." Arminian readers note that he names the man of God's disobedience, though he says nothing of his own deception.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the old prophet recognizes God's hand in the event. His interpretation affirms the reliability of God's word, even as his own role remains morally troubling.

verses.text: He said to his sons, saying, “Saddle the donkey for me,” and they saddled it.
verses.arminianNotes: He again has his donkey saddled. Arminian readers note the parallel with verse 13; the same man who rode out to bring the prophet back now rides out to bring back his body.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the somber echo of the earlier ride. What began as an invitation to a meal ends in a journey to recover a body, a vivid picture of the cost of disobedience.

verses.text: He went and found his body thrown on the path, and the donkey and the lion standing by the body. The lion had not eaten the body nor mauled the donkey.
verses.arminianNotes: The lion has not eaten the body or harmed the donkey. Arminian readers see God's restraint even in judgment, preserving the body for burial and dignity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the lion's unnatural restraint confirms God's control over every detail. Judgment comes exactly as spoken, and no further than God permits.

verses.text: The prophet took up the body of the man of God, and laid it on the donkey, and brought it back. He came to the city of the old prophet to mourn, and to bury him.
verses.arminianNotes: The old prophet brings the body back to mourn and bury him. Arminian readers note that he takes responsibility for honoring the dead man, perhaps out of grief or remorse, though the text does not say.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the old prophet's care for the body shows respect for the man of God and his message. God's servant, though disciplined, is honored in burial.

verses.text: He laid his body in his own grave; and they mourned over him, saying, “Alas, my brother!”
verses.arminianNotes: He lays the body in his own grave and mourns, "Alas, my brother!" Arminian readers note the grief in this lament and the bond the old prophet now claims with the man he deceived.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the man of God is buried away from his fathers, as the word said, yet with honor. The lament acknowledges him as a true servant of God despite his failure.

verses.text: After he had buried him, he spoke to his sons, saying, “When I am dead, bury me in the tomb in which the man of God is buried. Lay my bones beside his bones.
verses.arminianNotes: The old prophet asks to be buried beside the man of God. Arminian readers see him identifying with the faithful message of the man from Judah, perhaps seeking to align himself with God's truth at last.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Kings 23:18 records Josiah sparing these bones, "with the bones of the prophet who came out of Samaria." The old prophet's request is honored long after.

verses.text: For the saying which he cried by the LORD’s word against the altar in Bethel, and against all the houses of the high places which are in the cities of Samaria, will surely happen.”
verses.arminianNotes: The saying against Bethel "will surely happen." Arminian readers note that the old prophet now affirms the very word he once undermined.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the old prophet's confession anticipates 2 Kings 23. God's word against the high places stands sure, and even those who resisted it end up bearing witness to it.

verses.text: After this thing, Jeroboam didn’t turn from his evil way, but again made priests of the high places from among all the people. Whoever wanted to, he consecrated him, that there might be priests of the high places.
verses.arminianNotes: "Jeroboam didn't turn from his evil way" but kept appointing priests at will. Arminian readers see a king who received warning, judgment, and mercy, yet freely chose to persist in sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that despite a sign, a withered hand, and its healing, Jeroboam's heart remains unchanged. Outward displays of power do not by themselves produce repentance.

verses.text: This thing became sin to the house of Jeroboam, even to cut it off and to destroy it from off the surface of the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: This sin becomes the ruin of Jeroboam's house. Arminian readers note that the consequences follow a pattern of persistent choices, fulfilling the conditional warning given when Jeroboam first received the kingdom (11:38).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the destruction of Jeroboam's house is later carried out by Baasha "according to the saying of the LORD" (15:29). God's word of judgment governs the rise and fall of dynasties.
